los.text: Describe the effects of rheumatoid arthritis and its treatments on patients' daily lives.
los.html:
AreaEffects of RAEffects of treatment
PhysicalPain, morning stiffness, fatigue (often the most disabling), reduced hand function (dressing, jars, writing), mobility, deformity, sleep disturbanceNausea and mouth ulcers (methotrexate), infections, hair thinning, injection reactions, steroid side effects
PsychologicalDepression and anxiety (common), body image, loss of identityWorry about side effects, needle anxiety
Work and financesReduced hours, job loss, benefitsTime off for appointments and regular blood monitoring
Social and familyIsolation, relationships, intimacy, caring rolesAlcohol limits on methotrexate; pregnancy planning (methotrexate and leflunomide are teratogenic)
HealthHigher cardiovascular risk, osteoporosisVaccinations (no live vaccines on biologics; annual flu, pneumococcal, non-live shingles vaccine)
  • Support: rheumatology nurse specialist (advice line, flare plans)
    • physio (exercise, joint protection)
    • OT (aids, adaptations, splints)
    • podiatry
    • psychology
    • self-management education
    • patient groups (NRAS, Versus Arthritis).

los.text: Know the pathophysiology, clinical features, investigation and management of rheumatoid arthritis
los.html:
Epidemiology~1% of adults, women ~3:1, peak 30–50; HLA-DR4 (shared epitope) and smoking (drives citrullination).
Pathophysiology
  • Loss of tolerance to citrullinated proteins
  • → anti-CCP antibodies (and rheumatoid factor)
  • → synovitis (T cells, B cells, macrophages releasing TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1)
  • → synovial hyperplasia (pannus) invades cartilage and bone
  • → erosions (RANKL-activated osteoclasts)
  • → deformity
  • Systemic inflammation → fatigue, anaemia, accelerated atherosclerosis.
Clinical features
Symmetrical polyarthritis of the MCPs, PIPs, wrists and MTPs (DIPs spared); morning stiffness >30–60 min, better with activity
Deformities: ulnar deviation, swan neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb, wrist subluxation, MTP subluxation
  • Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules
  • Interstitial lung disease
  • Pleural effusion
  • Dry eyes (secondary Sjögren's)
  • Scleritis
  • Pericarditis
  • Vasculitis
  • Felty's syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia)
  • Anaemia of chronic disease
  • Carpal tunnel
  • Atlantoaxial subluxation (care with intubation)
  • Amyloidosis
InvestigationFinding
Anti-CCP (ACPA)~70% sensitive, ~95% specific; predicts erosive disease
Rheumatoid factor~70% positive but not specific (Sjögren's, infection, elderly)
ESR/CRP, FBCRaised; anaemia of chronic disease, thrombocytosis
X-ray hands and feetSoft tissue swelling, periarticular osteopenia, joint space loss, erosions, subluxation
UltrasoundSynovitis (power Doppler)
Pre-treatmentFBC, LFT, U&E, hepatitis B and C, HIV, CXR (before methotrexate)
Classification
  • ACR/EULAR 2010 (score ≥6/10: joints involved, serology, acute-phase reactants, duration ≥6 weeks).
  • DAS28 monitors activity (>5.1 high, <3.2 low, <2.6 remission).
Management (NICE NG100)
  • Urgent rheumatology referral if persistent synovitis (seen within 3 weeks)
  • Start a conventional DMARD within 3 months of symptoms: methotrexate first line (or leflunomide, sulfasalazine; hydroxychloroquine for mild disease) with short-term bridging steroids
  • Treat to target (remission or low activity, monthly review)
  • Add or combine DMARDs
  • If inadequate response to ≥2 DMARDs
  • Biologic or targeted therapy: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab: screen for TB and hepatitis)
  • Rituximab (anti-CD20)
  • Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor)
  • Abatacept (T-cell co-stimulation)
  • JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib: caution with VTE, cardiovascular risk, age >65, smokers)
  • Steroids for flares (IM or intra-articular)
  • NSAIDs for symptoms with a PPI
  • CV risk management, bone protection, vaccinations, smoking cessation
  • Surgery for damaged joints.
DMARDKey monitoring / adverse effects
Methotrexate (once weekly) + folic acid (on a different day)
  • Nausea, mouth ulcers, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis, teratogenic
  • Avoid trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole (marrow toxicity)
  • FBC, LFT, U&E every 2 weeks initially, then every 3 months
SulfasalazineRash, myelosuppression, hepatitis, reversible oligospermia, orange urine; safe in pregnancy
LeflunomideHypertension, hepatotoxicity, diarrhoea, teratogenic (long washout)
HydroxychloroquineRetinopathy (annual eye screening after 5 years); safe in pregnancy

los.text: Link the clinical features, investigation and management of metabolic bone diseases including: osteoporosis, osteomalacia / rickets, Paget's disease of bone
sessions: Investigation and management of bone diseases
los.html:
OsteoporosisOsteomalacia / ricketsPaget's disease of bone
PathologyLow bone mass and poor microarchitecture; normal mineralisationDefective mineralisation of osteoid (vitamin D deficiency)Disordered remodelling: excessive osteoclast resorption then chaotic osteoblast formation → large, weak, deformed woven/mosaic bone
CausesAge, menopause, steroids (see 219)Low vitamin D: poor sunlight, dark skin, covered clothing, diet, malabsorption (coeliac), CKD, liver disease, enzyme-inducing drugs; X-linked hypophosphataemiaOver 50, family history (SQSTM1); common in the UK
ClinicalFragility fractures (hip, vertebra, wrist); no symptoms otherwise
  • Adults: bone pain, tenderness, proximal myopathy (waddling gait), fractures, Looser's zones (pseudofractures).
  • Children: bowed legs, knock knees, rachitic rosary, wide wrists, frontal bossing, delayed walking, hypocalcaemic tetany/seizures
  • Often asymptomatic (raised ALP)
  • Bone pain
  • Deformity (bowed tibia, enlarged skull)
  • Warm skin over bone
  • Fractures
  • OA
  • Deafness (VIII compression)
  • Spinal stenosis
  • Rarely high-output heart failure or osteosarcoma
BloodsNormal Ca, PO₄, ALP, PTHLow/normal Ca, low PO₄, high ALP, low 25-OH vitamin D, high PTHIsolated very high ALP, normal Ca and PO₄
ImagingDEXA T ≤ −2.5Looser's zones; rickets: cupped, frayed metaphysesMixed lytic/sclerotic, cortical thickening, bone enlargement; isotope bone scan shows extent
TreatmentBisphosphonates etc.Vitamin D (colecalciferol loading then maintenance) + calcium; in CKD, active vitamin D (alfacalcidol, calcitriol)IV zoledronic acid (single dose) for bone pain; analgesia; surgery
  • Related: primary hyperparathyroidism (high Ca, low PO₄, high PTH: osteitis fibrosa cystica), CKD–mineral bone disorder (low Ca, high PO₄, very high PTH).

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of corticosteroids to be able to use them safely and effectively in the treatment of a range of conditions
los.html:
• Mechanism: glucocorticoids enter cells and bind the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor, which moves to the nucleus and changes gene transcription: switches on anti-inflammatory genes (e.g. annexin-1 → inhibits phospholipase A2 → fewer prostaglandins and leukotrienes) and switches off pro-inflammatory genes (blocks NF-κB and AP-1 → less IL-1, IL-6, TNF, COX-2)
    • also lymphocyte apoptosis, fewer eosinophils, raised neutrophil count (demargination), and metabolic effects.
DrugGlucocorticoid potencyMineralocorticoidEquivalent dose
Hydrocortisone1120 mg
Prednisolone40.85 mg
Methylprednisolone50.54 mg
Dexamethasone~25~00.75 mg
FludrocortisoneLowHighMineralocorticoid replacement
  • Uses: inflammatory and autoimmune disease (RA flares, PMR, GCA, SLE, vasculitis, IBD)
    • asthma/COPD exacerbations
    • allergy (adjunct)
    • cerebral oedema and meningitis (dexamethasone)
    • adrenal insufficiency (hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone)
    • chemotherapy and antiemesis
    • transplant
    • fetal lung maturation
    • Bell's palsy
    • croup
    • severe COVID-19.
    • Routes: oral, IV, IM, intra-articular, inhaled, topical, rectal.
Adverse effects
Metabolic: hyperglycaemia/diabetes, weight gain, central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, fluid retention, hypokalaemia, hypertension
Musculoskeletal: osteoporosis, avascular necrosis (femoral head), proximal myopathy, growth suppression in children
Immune: infections (masked signs), reactivation of TB/VZV
Skin: thinning, bruising, striae, poor wound healing, acne
Eyes: cataracts, glaucoma
GI: peptic ulcer (especially with NSAIDs)
CNS: insomnia, mood change, psychosis
Endocrine: adrenal suppression → adrenal crisis if stopped suddenly
  • Safe use: lowest effective dose for the shortest time, morning dosing
    • bone protection for ≥3 months of treatment (especially ≥65 or previous fracture: bisphosphonate, calcium and vitamin D)
    • PPI if GI risk
    • monitor BP, glucose, weight
    • steroid emergency card
    • sick day rules (double the dose with fever, IM hydrocortisone if vomiting)
    • taper rather than stopping abruptly after >3 weeks, high doses or repeated courses
    • adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia) → IV hydrocortisone 100 mg
    • avoid live vaccines on high doses
    • non-immune patients exposed to chickenpox need assessment.

los.text: Know the clinical features, investigation and management of a range of connective tissue diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, inflammatory muscle disease, Sjögren's syndrome).
sessions: Investigation and management of connective tissue disorders
los.html:
DiseaseFeaturesInvestigationsManagement
SLE
  • Young women (9:1), more common in Black and Asian people
  • Malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, discoid rash, oral ulcers, alopecia, non-erosive arthritis, serositis, lupus nephritis, cytopenias/haemolysis, seizures/psychosis, Raynaud's, fatigue, fever
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome (VTE, miscarriage)
  • ANA (sensitive ~95%)
  • Anti-dsDNA (specific, tracks activity and nephritis)
  • Anti-Sm
  • Low C3/C4 (active disease)
  • High ESR with normal CRP (high CRP suggests infection or serositis)
  • FBC
  • U&E
  • Urine dip and PCR
  • Antiphospholipid antibodies
  • Hydroxychloroquine for all, sun protection, NSAIDs, steroids, azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate (nephritis), cyclophosphamide, belimumab, rituximab, anifrolumab
  • CV risk
  • Pregnancy planning (anti-Ro → congenital heart block)
Systemic sclerosis
  • Limited cutaneous (CREST): Calcinosis, Raynaud's, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia
  • Skin distal to elbows/knees and face
  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension later.
  • Diffuse cutaneous: proximal skin, early ILD, scleroderma renal crisis (malignant hypertension, AKI), GI, cardiac
ANA; anticentromere (limited), anti-Scl-70 (diffuse, ILD), anti-RNA polymerase III (renal crisis); PFTs, HRCT, echo, BP, U&E
  • Raynaud's: nifedipine, iloprost, sildenafil
  • PPI
  • ACE inhibitor for renal crisis
  • Mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide, nintedanib for ILD
  • Endothelin antagonists for PAH
  • Avoid high-dose steroids (renal crisis)
Inflammatory myopathy (polymyositis, dermatomyositis)
  • Symmetrical proximal weakness (rising from a chair, stairs, combing hair), myalgia, dysphagia
  • DM skin: heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, shawl sign, mechanic's hands
  • ILD (anti-Jo-1)
  • DM linked to cancer
CK very high, EMG, MRI, muscle biopsy, myositis antibodies, cancer screenHigh-dose steroids + methotrexate/azathioprine, IVIG, rituximab
Sjögren's syndromeDry eyes and dry mouth, parotid swelling, fatigue, arthralgia; primary or secondary (RA, SLE); lymphoma riskAnti-Ro, anti-La, RF, ANA; Schirmer's test (<5 mm in 5 min); lip biopsyArtificial tears and saliva, pilocarpine, dental care, hydroxychloroquine
  • Raynaud's phenomenon: white → blue → red colour change of digits
    • primary (young, symmetrical, no ulcers) vs secondary (older onset, ulcers, abnormal nailfold capillaries, positive ANA: CTD).

los.text: Know the clinical features, investigation and management of vasculitis (temporal arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, Wegener's granulomatosis, polyarteritis nodosa).
los.html:
• Chapel Hill classification by vessel size: large (GCA, Takayasu), medium (PAN, Kawasaki), small: ANCA-associated (GPA, MPA, EGPA) and immune-complex (IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemic, anti-GBM).
ConditionFeaturesInvestigationsManagement
Giant cell (temporal) arteritis
  • >50, new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual disturbance (amaurosis fugax, diplopia, sudden blindness), fever, weight loss
  • Overlaps with PMR
ESR/CRP high, temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) or biopsy (skip lesions; within 2 weeks of starting steroids), FBC (anaemia, thrombocytosis)
  • Start prednisolone 40–60 mg immediately (don't wait for tests)
  • Visual loss → IV methylprednisolone
  • Same-day specialist review
  • PPI, bone protection
  • Tocilizumab if relapsing
  • Taper over 1–2 years
Polymyalgia rheumatica
  • >50, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness (morning >45 min), fatigue, raised ESR/CRP
  • Dramatic response to prednisolone 15 mg within days
  • Ask about GCA symptoms
ESR/CRP; exclude mimics (CK normal, RF, myeloma screen, TFTs, calcium)Prednisolone 15 mg, tapered over 1–2 years; bone protection
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)Small vessel necrotising granulomatous: upper airway (sinusitis, epistaxis, crusting, saddle nose), lungs (nodules, cavities, haemoptysis), kidneys (rapidly progressive GN), purpurac-ANCA (PR3), urine dip (blood, protein), U&E, CXR/CT, biopsyHigh-dose steroids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange for severe disease; maintenance rituximab/azathioprine
Polyarteritis nodosa
  • Medium vessel
  • Linked to hepatitis B
  • Fever, weight loss, mononeuritis multiplex, livedo reticularis, skin ulcers, hypertension and renal infarcts (not GN), mesenteric ischaemia, testicular pain
  • ANCA negative
Angiography (microaneurysms), biopsy, hepatitis B serologySteroids + cyclophosphamide; antivirals if hepatitis B

los.text: Link the clinical aspects, investigation and management of rheumatoid arthritis.
los.html:
• Linking it together (example): a 45-year-old woman who smokes has 3 months of symmetrical swelling of the MCPs and PIPs with 1 hour of morning stiffness.
StepFinding / action
ClinicalSynovitis (positive MCP squeeze test), DIPs spared, no psoriasis
InvestigationAnti-CCP positive, RF positive, CRP 30; X-rays show periarticular osteopenia (no erosions yet)
DiagnosisSeropositive RA (ACR/EULAR ≥6)
Management
  • Urgent rheumatology
  • Methotrexate weekly + folic acid, bridging steroid
  • DAS28 monthly to target
  • Stop smoking
  • CV risk
  • Vaccinations
  • Patient education, MDT
If inadequate responseCombination DMARDs → biologic after TB and hepatitis screening
Differential of inflammatory polyarthritis
  • Viral arthritis (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B/C, chikungunya)
  • Psoriatic arthritis (DIPs, dactylitis, nail changes)
  • SLE (non-erosive)
  • Polyarticular gout/CPPD
  • Reactive arthritis
  • PMR (older, girdle pain)
  • OA of the hands (DIPs, Heberden's nodes; brief stiffness).
PrognosisPoor prognostic factors are anti-CCP/RF positivity, early erosions, high inflammatory markers, many joints, smoking and extra-articular disease, which justify early aggressive treatment.

los.text: To go over questions submitted in advance following neuro SDL
los.html:
• Neuro SDL question review (see week 221 LOs 16–31): common areas to consolidate:
TopicKey points
TremorEssential (postural/action, symmetrical, alcohol helps, propranolol) vs Parkinsonian (rest, asymmetrical, bradykinesia)
Parkinson'sBradykinesia + tremor/rigidity; levodopa; never stop abruptly; avoid metoclopramide/haloperidol
HeadacheRed flags (thunderclap, fever, new >50, raised ICP features); migraine (triptan + NSAID; propranolol/topiramate/amitriptyline); cluster (oxygen, SC sumatriptan, verapamil)
MSOptic neuritis, INO, Lhermitte's; MRI + oligoclonal bands; relapses: methylprednisolone; DMTs
Neuro-ophthalmologyPainful III palsy with dilated pupil = aneurysm; papilloedema → image before LP; GCA → steroids now
Bulbar vs pseudobulbar palsyLMN (wasted fasciculating tongue) vs UMN (spastic tongue, brisk jaw jerk, emotional lability)

los.text: Differentiate between shockable and non-shockable cardiac rhythms and explain the clinical significance of each in the context of cardiac arrest management
los.html:
RhythmECGShockable?Clinical significance
Ventricular fibrillationChaotic, irregular deflections, no identifiable QRS (coarse or fine)YesEarly defibrillation is the main determinant of survival (each minute of delay lowers survival substantially)
Pulseless VTBroad, regular complexes, no pulseYesAs VF
AsystoleFlat line (check leads, gain; P waves only may respond to pacing)NoCPR, adrenaline ASAP, reversible causes; poor prognosis
PEAOrganised electrical activity without a pulseNoSearch for reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts) is critical: hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, PE
  • Shockable rhythms have a better prognosis if shocked quickly; non-shockable rhythms depend on high-quality CPR and treating the underlying cause.

los.text: Perform adult resuscitation competently, adhering to current UK Resuscitation Council guidelines, including team roles, airway management, defibrillation, and drug administration
los.html:
• Team roles: team leader (hands off, overview, decisions, closed-loop communication)
    • airway
    • compressors (rotate every 2 minutes)
    • defibrillator operator
    • IV/IO access and drugs
    • scribe/timekeeper
    • runner
    • brief before if possible, debrief after.
ElementResuscitation Council UK (2021)
CPR
  • 30:2 until airway secured, then continuous compressions with 10 breaths/min
  • Depth 5–6 cm, rate 100–120/min, full recoil
  • Minimise pauses (<5 s for rhythm checks and shocks)
Airway
  • Adjuncts and bag-valve-mask
  • Supraglottic airway (i-gel)
  • Tracheal intubation only by skilled operators
  • Waveform capnography to confirm placement, monitor CPR quality and detect ROSC (sudden rise in ETCO₂)
Defibrillation
  • Shockable: shock (biphasic, 150–360 J per device), resume CPR immediately for 2 min
  • Witnessed, monitored VF/pVT: up to 3 stacked shocks
Drugs
  • Adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO: non-shockable as soon as possible
  • Shockable after the 3rd shock
  • Then every 3–5 min
  • Amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd shock, 150 mg after the 5th
Reversible causes
  • 4 Hs: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and other metabolic, hypothermia
  • 4 Ts: thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary: consider thrombolysis), tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins
  • Point-of-care ultrasound if skilled
After ROSCABCDE, SpO₂ 94–98%, normal PaCO₂, 12-lead ECG (PCI if STEMI), MAP >65 mmHg, glucose control, prevent fever for 72 h, ICU
StoppingTeam decision considering duration, rhythm, reversible causes and patient wishes (DNACPR, ReSPECT)

los.text: Perform structured foot and ankle examination
sessions: Lower limb MSK exam – Foot and Ankle - applied clinical reasoning
los.html:
StepDetail
Look (standing)
  • Alignment: hallux valgus, lesser toe deformities, pes planus/cavus
  • From behind: hindfoot valgus/varus, "too many toes" sign
  • Gait
  • Tiptoe (heels should invert) and heel walking
  • Footwear wear
Look (lying)Skin (ulcers, calluses, colour, hair loss), nails, swelling, scars, deformity (claw, hammer, mallet toes)
Feel
  • Temperature, pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial), capillary refill
  • Tenderness: malleoli, base of 5th metatarsal, navicular, ankle joint line, Achilles (gap, thickening), plantar fascia origin, metatarsal heads (squeeze test)
MoveAnkle dorsiflexion (~20°) and plantarflexion (~50°); subtalar inversion and eversion; midfoot; 1st MTP (dorsiflexion)
Special testsSimmonds' (calf squeeze) test (Achilles rupture), anterior drawer (ATFL), Mulder's click (Morton's neuroma), single heel raise (tibialis posterior), Silfverskiöld (gastrocnemius tightness)
NeurovascularSensation incl. 10 g monofilament, vibration, ankle reflex, pulses
FinishKnee and lumbar spine; ABPI; footwear

los.text: Analyse clinical findings in the context of anatomical knowledge to identify potential underlying pathologies affecting the foot and ankle.
sessions: Lower limb MSK exam – Foot and Ankle - applied clinical reasoning
los.html:

Inversion injury, lateral swelling, tender in front of the lateral malleolusAnterior talofibular ligamentLateral ankle sprain
Bony tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of a malleolus, base of 5th metatarsal, navicular, or can't weight-bear 4 stepsOttawa rules positive → X-ray for fracture
Big toe deviated laterally with a bunion1st MTPHallux valgus
Painful stiff big toe, dorsal bump1st MTP osteoarthritisHallux rigidus
Burning pain and numbness between the 3rd and 4th toes, Mulder's clickInterdigital nerveMorton's neuroma
Acute red hot swollen 1st MTPGout
Flattened arch, "too many toes", can't do a single heel raiseTibialis posterior tendonTibialis posterior dysfunction (adult flatfoot)
High arch with claw toesNeurologicalPes cavus: CMT, Friedreich's, spinal dysraphism
Insensate foot, ulcer over metatarsal heads; hot swollen deformed midfootSensory neuropathyDiabetic neuropathic ulcer; Charcot neuroarthropathy
Burning sole, Tinel's behind the medial malleolusPosterior tibial nerveTarsal tunnel syndrome
MTP squeeze tenderness, symmetricalMTP synovitisRheumatoid arthritis
Forefoot pain in a runner, tender metatarsal shaftStress fracture

los.text: Formulate an appropriate plan for further investigation or referral, based on clinical findings and current guidelines.
sessions: Lower limb MSK exam – Foot and Ankle - applied clinical reasoning
los.html:
SituationPlan
Ankle injury meeting Ottawa rulesX-ray; fracture clinic
Achilles ruptureSame-day ED/orthopaedics; equinus boot or cast (or surgery)
Diabetic foot ulcer or suspected Charcot
  • Urgent referral to the MDT diabetic foot service (within 1 working day)
  • Emergency if spreading infection, sepsis or critical ischaemia
  • X-ray/MRI (osteomyelitis), ABPI, HbA1c
GoutClinical diagnosis or joint aspiration (negatively birefringent crystals); urate 2–4 weeks after the attack
Plantar fasciitisConservative: stretching, supportive footwear, insoles, weight loss, analgesia; physio; steroid injection if persistent
Hallux valgus / rigidusFootwear, orthotics; orthopaedic referral if pain limits function
Morton's neuromaWider footwear, metatarsal pad; ultrasound/MRI, injection, surgery
Tibialis posterior dysfunctionOrthotics, physio; orthopaedics if progressive
Inflammatory arthritisUrgent rheumatology
Arterial disease, ulcersABPI, vascular referral
NeuropathyMonofilament testing, HbA1c, B12; podiatry
Stress fracture, osteomyelitis, tendon pathologyMRI; ultrasound for tendons and neuromas

los.text: Clearly and concisely present clinical findings from a musculoskeletal examination using appropriate medical terminology and structure.
sessions: Lower limb MSK exam – Foot and Ankle - applied clinical reasoning
los.html:
Example
  • "I examined Mr X's right ankle and foot.
  • Standing, there was a normal arch and hindfoot alignment; he could not perform a single heel raise on the right.
  • There was swelling over the posterior ankle with a palpable gap about 4 cm above the calcaneal insertion.
  • Simmonds' test was positive on the right.
  • Ankle range was otherwise preserved, pulses were present and sensation intact.
  • In summary, these findings are consistent with an acute right Achilles tendon rupture.
  • I'd refer him to orthopaedics today and place him in an equinus boot."
Structure
  • Look → feel → move → special tests → neurovascular → summary → plan
  • Use precise terms (hindfoot valgus, pes planus/cavus, hallux valgus, dorsiflexion/plantarflexion in degrees, tenderness at named landmarks).

los.text: Predict the effects of pathology on the anatomy of the cardiovascular and respiratory system
los.html:
PathologyAnatomical changeEffects you can predict
Left ventricular hypertrophy (hypertension, aortic stenosis)Thick LV wall, stiff ventricleDiastolic dysfunction, ischaemia (more muscle, same arteries), apex beat heaving but not displaced
Dilated heart / LV failureDilated LV, stretched mitral ringDisplaced apex, functional mitral regurgitation, pulmonary oedema (Kerley B lines, bat-wing shadowing, upper lobe diversion)
Right heart failure / cor pulmonaleDilated RV and RARaised JVP, hepatomegaly (hepatic veins → IVC), ankle oedema, ascites
Left atrial enlargement (mitral stenosis)Big LA behind the heartSplayed carina, double right heart border, dysphagia (oesophagus), hoarseness (left recurrent laryngeal stretched: Ortner's), AF and thrombus
Pericardial effusion / tamponadeFluid in the fibrous sacGlobular "water-bottle" heart, Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus
Aortic aneurysm / dissection (arch)Dilated archCompresses the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarse), trachea, oesophagus; dissection can block coronary, carotid, subclavian or renal branches
CoarctationNarrowing near the ligamentum arteriosumRadiofemoral delay; collateral intercostal arteries cause rib notching
Lung cancer (apex: Pancoast)Tumour at the thoracic inletHorner's (sympathetic chain), T1 root (wasting of hand muscles), brachial plexus pain
Central lung cancer / mediastinal nodesMass at the hilumSVC obstruction (facial swelling, dilated chest veins), phrenic palsy (raised hemidiaphragm), recurrent laryngeal palsy (left)
Pleural effusionFluid in the pleural spaceStony dull base, reduced breath sounds, mediastinum pushed away (large)
Pneumothorax / tensionAir in the pleural spaceCollapse; tension pushes the trachea and mediastinum away, kinks great veins → shock
Lobar collapseVolume lossTrachea and mediastinum pulled towards the affected side; raised hemidiaphragm
COPD / emphysemaHyperinflation, bullaeFlat diaphragms, barrel chest, more than 6 anterior ribs visible, narrow heart
AspirationRight main bronchus wider, shorter, more verticalAspiration pneumonia in the right lower lobe (upright) or posterior segments (lying)
  • Approach: think about where the structure lies
    • what it touches (nerves, vessels, airways, oesophagus) and what happens if it grows
    • shrinks
    • blocks or bleeds.
